exercise.given: No code is required unless the lesson explicitly says to run verification. You are given a three-sentence answer shape, so you do not need to invent a speech structure.

starter.label: Fill in this three-sentence interview frame
starter.content:
Definition: ___
Why it matters: ___
OrderFlow example: ___

steps: Give the definition in one sentence.
Say why the concept matters in one sentence.
Point to one concrete OrderFlow example.
Say the three sentences aloud, then reveal the answer and correct only what was missing.
exercise.run: Say the answer aloud before revealing it; use the final verification command only for practical-check lessons.
exercise.expected: You give a correct 20–30 second answer containing a definition, why it matters, and one OrderFlow example.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Use an external source only for one named gap, write the single correction it adds to your mental model, and return to OrderFlow to apply it. Do not replace the coherent tutorial path with a new course immediately before the interview.

exercise.task: Close the page and explain what OrderFlow became across eight stages. Stop when the explanation is coherent rather than chasing perfect recall.

exercise.answer: OrderFlow grew from variables and control flow into an encapsulated domain, asynchronous application service, authenticated ASP.NET Core API, EF Core/SQLite persistence, tested architecture, and a measured scaling story. A coherent explanation plus safe reasoning is the goal—not pretending to remember every API.
